prompt: A British tech company opens a Paris office. Their employment contracts, written in English common law style, specify at-will termination with a notice period. French labour law makes termination nearly impossible without cause and requires works council consultation. The company's London lawyers say the contracts are clear. The French employees' representative says the contracts are void under French law regardless of what language they're written in. A Franco-British employee who negotiated her own hybrid contract is now the template everyone wants but the legal team says can't scale. The CEO, who speaks schoolboy French, keeps saying 'it's the same thing, just different words'. It is not the same thing.

A British food delivery startup enters the French market using AI to optimise restaurant prep times and delivery routes. In London, this means faster service — restaurants pre-cook popular items based on predicted demand. French restaurant owners revolt: the algorithm treats a cassoulet like a pizza, optimising for speed over technique. A Michelin-starred chef says the app is 'the death of cuisine'. A delivery rider in the banlieues says the app is the only reason his immigrant-run restaurant gets any customers at all. The startup's data shows French users order 40% faster when food arrives faster, but rate the food 15% lower. The algorithm doesn't have a variable for 'was this made with care'.

A Brazilian museum holds Incan artefacts that were looted by Portuguese colonists from what is now Peru (then under Spanish colonial control). Peru wants them back. Brazil says they were legally acquired under Portuguese colonial law. Spain argues they were stolen from Spanish territory first. The indigenous Quechua community whose ancestors made the objects says all three colonial successor states are arguing over stolen goods and none of them have standing. A museum conservator notes the artefacts will deteriorate without the climate-controlled environment the museum provides. The Quechua community's proposed heritage centre in Cusco doesn't have climate control. What does restitution look like when everyone's claim is built on someone else's dispossession?

The Tagus river rises in Spain and flows through Portugal to the Atlantic. Spain's intensive agriculture in the upper basin consumes so much water that by the time the river reaches Lisbon, it's a fraction of its historical volume. Portugal invokes the 1998 Albufeira Convention requiring minimum flows. Spain says its farmers depend on irrigation to survive EU agricultural competition. Portuguese fishermen at the river mouth say the reduced flow has collapsed the estuary ecosystem. A Spanish environmental activist agrees with Portugal but says the real villain is EU agricultural subsidies that incentivise water-intensive crops in a semi-arid landscape. Both countries need the river. Neither can have all of it.

A linguist builds a machine translation system between Hindi and Urdu. Grammatically they are the same language — Hindustani. But Hindi uses Devanagari script and borrows from Sanskrit; Urdu uses Nastaliq script and borrows from Persian/Arabic. Her 'translator' is essentially a script converter with vocabulary substitution. Hindu nationalists say this proves Urdu is just 'Hindi in foreign dress'. Pakistani linguists say Hindi is a colonial invention that stripped Urdu of its Islamic heritage. Her Bollywood-loving test users (who switch between Hindi and Urdu unconsciously in conversation) say the tool is useful and the politics are boring. A Partition survivor says the day Hindi and Urdu became different languages was the day his country broke in half. The linguist's data shows the languages are converging again through social media.

A Japanese calligraphy master teaches a workshop in Shanghai. Her art uses kanji — Chinese characters adopted into Japanese writing 1,500 years ago. Chinese students are fascinated but some find it strange: familiar characters used in unfamiliar ways, carrying unfamiliar cultural weight. The character 道 (dao/michi) means 'the way' in both traditions but carries Taoist philosophy in Chinese and bushido associations in Japanese. A Chinese art critic writes that Japanese calligraphy is 'derivative'. The calligrapher says 1,500 years of independent evolution makes it a distinct art form. A Korean student points out that Korea abandoned Chinese characters entirely and asks whether Japan's retention is cultural preservation or failure to decolonise. The characters themselves predate all three nations.

A joint Japanese-Chinese team is developing a high school history textbook for use in both countries. The Nanjing chapter is the immediate problem. Chinese historical consensus: 300,000 killed in a systematic massacre. Some Japanese historians' position: the number is lower, the events were war crimes but not genocide, and the figure has been politically inflated. Both sides have primary sources supporting their claims. The textbook team agrees on the documented facts but cannot agree on the framing. A Chinese historian says framing the numbers as 'disputed' is itself a form of denialism. A Japanese historian says accepting an unverifiable number sets a precedent that undermines all historical methodology. The students who will use this textbook were born 75 years after the events. What do they need to know, and how?

A digital humanities project is building an open-access archive of Islamic Golden Age manuscripts. Many key works were written in Arabic by Persian scholars — Avicenna (Ibn Sina) wrote the Canon of Medicine in Arabic, but was born in what is now Uzbekistan and spoke Persian at home. Iran claims him as Persian heritage. Arab scholars note the work's language and the civilisation that supported it were Arabic. A Turkish historian points out the manuscript was preserved in Ottoman libraries. The digitisation team must decide: metadata categories, attribution, language tags. Every cataloguing decision is a claim about whose civilisation produced the knowledge. A Pakistani PhD student using the archive just wants to find the text. She doesn't care who 'owns' Avicenna — she needs his pharmacology.

A Swahili-language cultural festival in Lamu, Kenya celebrates the coast's hybrid heritage — Bantu grammar with extensive Arabic vocabulary, Islamic architecture with African design, Arab trade routes that built Swahili city-states. A post-colonial scholar argues the festival romanticises Arab slave trading that devastated East African interior communities. An Omani-Kenyan family whose ancestors settled in Lamu 300 years ago says they are as African as anyone. A Swahili poet says the language itself is proof that cultures can merge without one dominating the other. A historian from the interior Kikuyu community says Swahili coastal culture was built on enslaving his ancestors, and the 'hybrid heritage' narrative erases that. The festival organiser, herself of mixed Arab-Bantu heritage, doesn't know which part of her history to apologise for.
